content:
Yesterday brought two contradictory reports about next year's 20th anniversary iPhone model, which is said to embody Apple's long-term vision of "a slab of glass."

Reports about what we can actually expect have diverged for some time, but yesterday's divergence was the starkest yet……

Current state

Former Apple design chief Jony Ive has often spoken of his long-term vision of eventually making the iPhone a single piece of glass, and it's widely believed that even after Ive's departure, Apple continues to push toward this vision.

While Apple generally doesn't celebrate anniversaries in a big way, the industry consensus is that they are aiming to get as close to this vision as possible by the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. This likely includes embedding Face ID under the display, and hiding the front camera under the display as well.

However, we've already seen contradictory reports about these expectations. The initial view was that this would be a standalone model, similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but newer reports indicate that the design will instead come to next year's iPhone Pro models.

By order, that would be the iPhone 19 Pro, though Apple may also want to skip a generation and name it the iPhone 20 to mark the anniversary.

Yesterday's conflicting reports

Things got even more muddled yesterday, when an analyst claimed that Apple had abandoned the idea of an all-glass iPhone next year.

However, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman quickly shot down that claim.

The more likely reality

The point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone doesn't have a single endpoint. Whatever they plan to deliver next year is just one or more steps toward that sci-fi vision of "a slab of glass."

The question isn't whether that goal can be achieved next year, but how many steps toward that vision Apple will take. But whether it's one step or several, this certainly won't be the final step in the iPhone's design evolution.

In fact, Gurman revealed that Apple has actually stepped back from how far they were originally hoping to achieve next year.

The Jefferies analyst most likely heard the same news, but later, and mistakenly thought the plan had been abandoned entirely.

My own expectation is that next year's design will be a major leap — comparable to the breakthrough of the original iPhone X — but that there will be further developments in the years after that. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will feature a big enough leap to warrant Apple adopting some kind of special branding strategy, such as marking it as the 20th anniversary iPhone (which I think is extremely unlikely), giving it some other special name, or skipping a generation to call it the iPhone 20.

What are your hopes? Share them in the comments.
